meaning: “Only ...”, always followed by a negative verb. It stresses that an amount is small or a range is narrow, with a feeling of “not enough” or “that's all”.
connection: Noun / quantity (+ particle) + しか + negative verb

senses.label: Only (a small amount)
senses.meaning: Limits a quantity and stresses “only this much”. The speaker feels it is too little. The form is negative, but the meaning is positive.
senses.connection: Quantity + しか + ない／ありません／〜ません
examples: I only have 1,000 yen in my wallet.
This shop only has three chairs.
I only slept four hours yesterday.

senses.label: Only (a limited range)
senses.meaning: Limits a person, thing, place, etc., and rules out everything else: “nothing but ...”. It can follow particles such as 「で」, 「に」 and 「から」.
senses.connection: Noun (+ で／に／から, etc.) + しか + negative verb
examples: I can only speak Japanese.
You can only buy this ticket at this station.
Only Tanaka came.

senses.label: No choice but to
senses.meaning: Dictionary form + 「しかない」 means “the only thing to do is ...” or “have no choice but to ...”.
senses.connection: Verb dictionary form + しかない／しかありません
examples: There are no buses, so I have no choice but to walk home.
There's nothing left to do but go for it.

notes: 「しか」 must be followed by a negative, yet the sentence means a positive “only”: 「千円しかない」 = “I have 1,000 yen (and that's all)”, not “I don't have 1,000 yen”. ✕「千円しかある」.
「しか」 replaces 「が」 and 「を」 — you can't stack them: ✕「水をしか飲まない」→ ○「水しか飲まない」. 「で」, 「に」 and 「から」 stay in front: 「駅でしか買えない」.
「しか」 carries a complaint that something is too little. Saying 「お土産を一つしかもらわなかった」 about a present sounds like grumbling; if you just want to state the fact, use 「だけ」: 「一つだけもらった」.

daily.title: Short on cash while shopping
daily.description: You realize in a shop you don't have enough money and quietly tell your friend.
daily.example: Sorry, I only have 1,000 yen on me right now.

daily.title: Describing your language skills
daily.description: Modestly saying which languages you speak when introducing yourself.
daily.example: I can only speak a little English.

daily.title: Missing the last train
daily.description: The last train has left, so you have to walk or take a taxi.
daily.example: There's no last train, so I'll have to take a taxi home.

work.title: Explaining low stock
work.description: A shop clerk tells a customer that only a few items are left.
work.example: I'm very sorry, we only have two in stock.

work.title: Running short on time in a meeting
work.description: The chair reminds everyone that little time is left.
work.example: We only have ten minutes left, so let's hurry.

etymology: 「しか」 is generally thought to come from an old adverb 「しか」 (然) meaning “so, like that”. It later became a limiting particle paired with a negative, and spread in everyday speech from the Edo period on.
formation: 「しか」 is a limiting particle that draws a boundary around the item in front of it; the negative 「ない」 then denies everything outside that boundary. Together they say “there is nothing except X”, which works out to “only X”. Because “only” is reached by denying everything else, the sentence has to be negative in form but positive in meaning. And since the speaker is focused on “nothing else”, a feeling of “too little, not enough” comes along naturally. 「〜しかない」 after a verb's dictionary form follows the same logic: “there is no (other path) except doing this” → “have no choice but to”.

similar.title: 〜だけ
similar.explanation: 「だけ」 limits the range objectively and works with both positive and negative predicates. 「しか〜ない」 requires a negative and adds the subjective feeling of “too little, not enough”. 「千円だけある」 is a neutral statement; 「千円しかない」 complains that it isn't enough.

similar.title: 〜のみ
similar.explanation: 「のみ」 also means “only” and takes a positive predicate, but it is written language, common on notices and in rules, e.g. 「現金のみ使用可」. In speech you'd say 「現金しか使えない」 or 「現金だけ」.

similar.title: 〜しかない (have no choice but to)
similar.explanation: Same origin: 「しか」 after a verb's dictionary form, followed by 「ない」, means “there is no other way than doing this”, i.e. “have no choice but to”, as in 「歩いて帰るしかない」. This entry, noun + 「しか〜ない」, limits things and amounts.

meaning: “Only, just”. Limits a range or amount, and can be followed by either a positive or a negative.
connection: Noun / quantity / plain form of verbs and adjectives + だけ

senses.label: Only, just
senses.meaning: Limits a person or thing: “just this, nothing else”. The tone is neutral and doesn't necessarily mean “too little”.
senses.connection: Noun + だけ (+ particle); 「だけ」 can replace 「が」 and 「を」, and 「だけを」 / 「だけが」 are also fine
examples: I only drink coffee in the morning.
I'm only telling you this.
I was the only one who didn't know.

senses.label: Only (an amount)
senses.meaning: After a quantity, it means “just (this many)”. It is more neutral and matter-of-fact than 「しか〜ない」.
senses.connection: Quantity + だけ
examples: Just one, please.
Please wait just a moment.
I've been to Japan only once.

senses.label: Just (doing something)
senses.meaning: After a verb or adjective, it means “only ..., nothing more”. Often used as 「〜だけです」 or 「〜だけで」.
senses.connection: Plain form of verbs and adjectives + だけ (だ／です)
examples: I'm just looking. I'm not buying.
I'm just a little tired.

notes: When 「だけ」 is used with a negative, the negative applies to that item itself: 「肉だけ食べない」 = “meat is the one thing I don't eat”. To say “I eat only meat”, use 「肉だけ食べる」 or 「肉しか食べない」 — mix them up and you say the exact opposite.
Saying 「これだけですか」 when you receive a present, help or a quote sounds like “Is that all?” and is very rude. Even if you only want to confirm the quantity, say 「こちらで全部でしょうか」.
「できるだけ」 means “as much as possible” and 「好きなだけ」 “as much as you like” — not “only”: 「できるだけ早く来て」 = “Please come as early as you can”, not “you may only come early”.
「だけど」 and 「だけれど」 mean “but”, not “only”: 「雨だけど行く」 = “It's raining, but I'll go”, not “only rain”.

daily.title: Browsing in a shop
daily.description: When a clerk comes over, you say you're just looking around.
daily.example: It's fine, I'm just looking.

daily.title: Ordering
daily.description: Ordering only one thing at a café.
daily.example: Just a coffee, please.

daily.title: Telling a friend a secret
daily.description: You want to share a secret with your close friend only.
daily.example: I'm only telling you this, okay?

work.title: Asking for the floor in a meeting
work.description: Asking for a little of everyone's time in a meeting.
work.example: Could I have just a moment of your time?

work.title: Confirming attendance
work.description: Reporting to your boss who will attend an event.
work.example: This time, only the department manager and I will attend.

etymology: 「だけ」 comes from the noun 「たけ」 (丈), meaning “height, length”. It came to mean “the full amount, the limit”, then became voiced as 「だけ」 to mean “limited to this”.
formation: 「だけ」 comes from the noun 「丈（たけ）」, originally “height, size, the full amount”. Attached to a noun or a quantity, it says “the amount goes this far and no further”, hence “only, just”. Because it marks the upper limit of a range and contains no negation itself, it can be followed by either a positive or a negative, and its tone is fairly objective. The same “full amount” sense also developed in another direction: 「できるだけ」 (the full amount you can do → as much as possible) and 「好きなだけ」 (the full amount you like → as much as you like).

similar.title: 〜しか〜ない
similar.explanation: 「しか」 must be followed by a negative and carries a sense of “too little”; 「だけ」 works with positives and negatives and sounds objective. 「三人だけ来た」 is a statement; 「三人しか来なかった」 complains that so few came.

similar.title: 〜のみ
similar.explanation: 「のみ」 means almost the same as 「だけ」 but is written language, seen on notices, in regulations and in the news (「会員のみ入場可」). In conversation use 「だけ」; 「のみ」 sounds stiff.

similar.title: 〜だけで
similar.explanation: Same origin: 「だけ」 + 「で」 means “just by ..., already ...”, stressing that this alone produces the result, as in 「見るだけで楽しい」. In this entry 「だけ」 simply limits the range.

similar.title: 〜だけ (extent)
similar.explanation: Same origin: the 「だけ」 in 「できるだけ」, 「好きなだけ」 and 「やれるだけやる」 means “to the full extent of ...”. It keeps the original sense of 「だけ」, “the full amount”, and does not mean “only”.

meaning: After an amount or a length of time, it means “about, around”. 「どのくらい」 asks “how much / how long”.
connection: Quantity + くらい／ぐらい; どの／どれ + くらい

senses.label: About (an amount)
senses.meaning: Gives a rough amount, price or distance: “about ..., around ...”. 「くらい」 and 「ぐらい」 mean the same and are interchangeable.
senses.connection: Number + counter + くらい／ぐらい
examples: It's about a ten-minute walk to the station.
This bag was about 5,000 yen.
About thirty people came to the party.

senses.label: About (a length of time)
senses.meaning: Gives a rough length of time, like “a few hours” or “a few days”. Note: use 「ごろ」 for a point in time and 「くらい」 for a length of time.
senses.connection: 〜時間／〜日／〜年, etc. + くらい／ぐらい
examples: I study for about two hours every day.
I lived in Japan for about a year.

senses.label: Asking how much
senses.meaning: 「どのくらい」 / 「どれぐらい」 ask about amount, time, distance or degree: “how much, how long, how far”.
senses.connection: どの／どれ + くらい／ぐらい (+ かかりますか, etc.)
examples: How long does it take to get to the airport?
How long have you been studying Japanese?

notes: Use 「ごろ」 for a point in time and 「くらい」 for a length of time: 「三時ごろ」 = around three o'clock, 「三時間くらい」 = about three hours. ✕「三時間ごろ」.
「くらい」 goes after the number, not before it: ✕「くらい十人来た」→ ○「十人くらい来た」. Before a noun, say 「十人くらいの学生」.
Giving a time or an amount to a client or superior with 「〜くらい」 sounds casual, even careless. In business say 「十分ほどお待ちください」, 「約五万円です」 or 「三日程度かかります」.

daily.title: Asking for directions
daily.description: Asking a passer-by how long it takes to get to the station.
daily.example: How long does it take to get to the station?

daily.title: Talking about your habits
daily.description: Telling a friend how much exercise you do every day.
daily.example: I run for about thirty minutes every morning.

daily.title: Talking about prices
daily.description: A friend asks how much something was, and you can only remember roughly.
daily.example: I think it was about 20,000 yen.

work.title: Estimating a schedule
work.description: Telling a client roughly how long a job will take.
work.example: We expect it to take about a week to complete.

work.title: Reporting attendance
work.description: Telling your boss roughly how many people came to an event.
work.example: About fifty people attended the information session.

etymology: 「くらい」 comes from the noun 「位（くらい）」, meaning “rank, grade”. It came to mean “degree, amount”, and then became a particle for rough amounts. 「ぐらい」 is its voiced form and spread in speech from the Edo period on.
formation: 「くらい」 comes from the noun 「位（くらい）」, originally “rank, position”. After a number it means “at the rank where this value sits” — not an exact point but “around this level”, hence “about”. Because it measures quantity, it attaches to things that can be counted or measured, such as amounts and durations; a clock time is a point, not a quantity, so it normally takes 「ごろ」 instead. 「どの＋くらい」 literally asks “at which rank?”, so it means “how much / how long?”. 「ぐらい」 is the voiced form; the meaning is the same.

similar.title: 〜ごろ
similar.explanation: 「ごろ」 follows a point in time (「七時ごろ」) and means around that moment; 「くらい」 follows an amount or a length of time (「七時間くらい」). You do hear 「七時くらい」 in speech, but the standard form is 「七時ごろ」.

similar.title: 〜ばかり (about)
similar.explanation: After a number, 「ばかり」 also means “about”, as in 「十日ばかり休んだ」, but it is more literary and a little old-fashioned. Everyday speech uses 「くらい」; formal settings prefer 「ほど」 or 「程度」.

similar.title: 〜くらい・〜ぐらい (degree)
similar.explanation: Same origin: after nouns and verbs it means “to the point of ...”, as in 「泣きたいくらい痛い」 (it hurts so much I could cry). This entry attaches only to numbers and gives an approximate value.

similar.title: 〜くらい・〜ぐらい (at least / trivializing)
similar.explanation: Same origin: 「挨拶くらいしなさい」 (at least say hello), 「それくらい自分でやって」 (do something that small yourself) — it means “a mere ..., at the very least”. Again, it is not about an approximate amount.

meaning: After a word for a point in time, it means “around, about” that time.
connection: Time noun (〜時・〜日・〜月・〜年, etc.) + ごろ (頃)

senses.label: Around (a clock time)
senses.meaning: Gives an approximate time: “around ... o'clock”. Often followed by 「に」, but 「に」 can be dropped.
senses.connection: 〜時／〜時半 + ごろ (に)
examples: I get up around seven every morning.
Let's meet at the station around 3:30.
I went to bed around eleven last night.

senses.label: Around (a date or period)
senses.meaning: After a date, month, season, year, etc., it gives an approximate period.
senses.connection: 〜日／〜月／〜年／週末／昼, etc. + ごろ
examples: Cherry blossoms bloom around April.
The package should arrive around the 10th.
I'll call you around noon.

senses.label: Asking roughly when
senses.meaning: 「いつごろ」 asks “around when?”. It is softer than 「いつ」 and doesn't ask for an exact time.
senses.connection: いつ + ごろ
examples: Around when did you come to Japan?

notes: 「ごろ」 attaches only to points in time, never to lengths of time: ✕「三時間ごろ待った」→ ○「三時間くらい待った」.
「ごろ」 is an approximate time, so it can't go with 「ちょうど」 (exactly): ✕「ちょうど三時ごろ」→ ○「ちょうど三時に」 or 「三時ごろ」.
On its own or after 「の」 it is read 「ころ」 and means “the time when ...”: 「子どもの頃（ころ）」 = when I was a child, not “approximately”. 「このごろ」 means “these days”.

daily.title: Making plans with a friend
daily.description: Setting a rough time to meet a friend.
daily.example: Okay, let's meet at the station around six.

daily.title: Saying when you'll be home
daily.description: Telling your family roughly when you'll be back before you go out.
daily.example: I'll be home around nine today.

daily.title: Planning a trip
daily.description: Talking with a friend about when to travel.
daily.example: Around when are you going this summer break?

work.title: Saying when you'll reply
work.description: Telling a client roughly when you'll get back to them.
work.example: I will contact you around next Wednesday.

work.title: Giving a delivery date
work.description: Telling a customer roughly when the goods will arrive.
work.example: We expect to deliver the product around the end of the month.

etymology: 「ごろ」 is the noun 「頃（ころ）」, voiced when attached to another word. 「頃」 means “time, period”. After a specific time, it means “around that time”, i.e. an approximate time.
formation: 「ごろ」 is the noun 「頃（ころ）」, voiced (rendaku) when it follows another word. 「頃」 originally means “time, period”, so 「七時頃」 is literally “the seven-o'clock period”. A period has some width, so the whole phrase means “around seven” — an approximate time. And because its core meaning is “a moment or period”, it attaches only to clock times, dates and seasons, never to lengths of time. 「いつ＋ごろ」 = “what period?”, asking roughly when.

similar.title: 〜くらい・〜ぐらい
similar.explanation: 「くらい」 gives an approximate amount or length of time (「二時間くらい」); 「ごろ」 gives only an approximate point in time (「二時ごろ」). Ask “around what time?” with 「何時ごろ」 and “how long?” with 「どのくらい」.

similar.title: 〜に (point in time)
similar.explanation: 「七時に」 means exactly at seven; 「七時ごろ（に）」 means around seven, with some leeway. Use 「に」 when the other person has to be on time (meetings, appointments), and 「ごろ」 when you only mean roughly.

meaning: Read 「じゅう」, it means “throughout, all over” or “within (a period)”. Read 「ちゅう」, it means “in the middle of, currently ...ing”.

senses.label: Throughout (time or space)
senses.meaning: Read 「じゅう」. With a time noun, it means “the whole ...”. With a place noun, it means “all over ...”.
senses.connection: 一日中・一年中・一晩中・世界中・日本中・家中, etc.
examples: It rained all day yesterday.
This song is popular all over the world.
I couldn't sleep all night.

senses.label: Within (a deadline)
senses.meaning: With 「今日」, 「今週」, 「今月」, etc., it sets a deadline: “by the end of ...”. Often used with 「に」. 「今日中」 is read 「きょうじゅう」; 「今週中」 can be read either way.
senses.connection: 今日中・今週中・今月中・午前中 + に
examples: Please hand in this report by the end of today.
I'll give you an answer by the end of this week.

senses.label: In the middle of
senses.meaning: Read 「ちゅう」. With an action noun, it means “currently ...ing” or “during ...”. Common on signs and when describing a status.
senses.connection: 会議中・授業中・仕事中・電話中・営業中・食事中, etc.
examples: The manager is in a meeting right now.
Please don't use your phone during class.
This shop is open 24 hours.

notes: A shop sign reading 「準備中」 means “getting ready — not open yet”; 「営業中」 is the one that means “open”. 「休憩中」 and 「会議中」 likewise mean “not available right now”, so don't take them as an invitation to walk in.
「〜中（ちゅう）」 attaches only to nouns, not directly to verbs: ✕「食べる中」→ ○「食事中」 or 「食べている」.
「〜中（じゅう）」 and 「〜の中（なか）」 mean different things: 「家中（いえじゅう）探した」 = I searched the whole house; 「家の中で探した」 = I searched inside the house.
When your boss says 「今日中に」, it is a deadline — “by the end of today (usually before you leave work)” — not “sometime today is fine”. Letting it slip to the next day is seen as breaking your word.

daily.title: Complaining about the weather
daily.description: Telling a friend it was hot all day.
daily.example: It was hot all day today, wasn't it?

daily.title: Reading a sign at a shop
daily.description: You see a sign at a shop entrance showing its status.
daily.example: They're still getting ready, so we can't go in yet.

daily.title: Looking for something
daily.description: You can't find your keys after searching the whole house.
daily.example: I looked all over the house, but my keys aren't anywhere.

work.title: Handling a phone call
work.description: A receptionist tells a caller that the person in charge is busy.
work.example: Tanaka is on another call at the moment.

work.title: Giving a deadline
work.description: Promising to finish something by a certain time.
work.example: We will send you the quote by the end of this week.

etymology: 「中」 is a loanword from Chinese. The reading 「ちゅう」 keeps the meaning “middle, within”, which extended to “in progress”. 「じゅう」 is a voiced variant that means “across the whole range”.
formation: 「中」 originally means “middle, inside”. Read 「ちゅう」, it keeps the sense of “being inside ...”: after action nouns such as 「会議」 or 「授業」 it means “inside a meeting” → in progress. Read 「じゅう」, it looks at “every spot within this range”, so 「一日中」 = every moment of the day → all day long, and 「世界中」 = every corner of the world → all over the world. 「今日中に」 means “within the range of today” → by the end of today. The same idea of “inside” splits into two readings and two uses depending on whether you look at “being in it” or “filling all of it”.

similar.title: 〜中（ちゅう／じゅう）
similar.explanation: The same suffix revisited at a higher level: at N3 you meet more combinations such as 「工事中」, 「話し中」, 「世界中」 and 「町中」. The meaning is the same as this entry, so review them together.

similar.title: 〜最中に
similar.explanation: 「最中」 is also built on 「中」 and means “right in the middle of ...”, usually followed by something unexpected: 「会議の最中に電話が鳴った」. 「〜中」 just describes being in a state; 「最中に」 stresses “right then, of all times”.

similar.title: 〜間・〜間に
similar.explanation: 「間（あいだ）」 also means “during ...” and can follow verbs (「寝ている間に」); 「〜中」 follows only nouns, is more concise, and is common on signs and in business. 「会議の間」 ≈ 「会議中」.

meaning: After a noun or pronoun referring to people, it marks the plural. It can also mean “... and others, ... and the rest”.
connection: Personal pronoun / noun for people + たち (達)

senses.label: Plural (people)
senses.meaning: Marks more than one person. Japanese nouns usually have no plural form, so 「たち」 is added when you want to stress “several people”.
senses.connection: 私・僕・あなた・君・彼・彼女・子ども・学生, etc. + たち
examples: We're in the same class.
The children are playing in the park.
The students listened to the teacher.

senses.label: ... and the others
senses.meaning: After a person's name, it means “that person and their group”. The others aren't necessarily the same kind of person.
senses.connection: Person's name (+ さん) + たち
examples: Tanaka and the others have already gone home.
Yesterday I went shopping with my mom and the others.

senses.label: Animals, etc. (affectionate)
senses.meaning: In principle it's for people, but you can use it for animals or plants you feel close to. It sounds warm and personifying.
senses.connection: 動物・ペット, etc. + たち
examples: Our cats are all doing well.

notes: 「〜たち」 means “a group represented by that person”, not necessarily several of the same kind: 「田中さんたち」 = Tanaka and the people with him, not “several Tanakas”.
「たち」 is not polite enough for teachers, clients and other superiors: ✕「先生たち」「お客様たち」→ ○「先生方（がた）」, 「お客様方」 or 「皆様」.
In principle 「たち」 is used only for people (and personified animals): ✕「本たち」「車たち」.
「友達」 is a single word and can refer to just one friend. ✕「友達たち」 sounds childish; for the plural just say 「友達」 or 「友人たち」.

daily.title: Introducing yourself and a friend
daily.description: Telling someone how you and your friend know each other.
daily.example: We're friends from university.

daily.title: Watching children
daily.description: Seeing a group of children playing in a park.
daily.example: The kids look like they're having fun.

daily.title: Saying who you're with
daily.description: Telling your family who you're with.
daily.example: I'm having dinner with Sato and the others right now.

work.title: Explaining inside the company
work.description: Used when introducing team members.
work.example: Our team has five people.

work.title: Welcoming new employees
work.description: Giving a speech at a welcome party for new staff.
work.example: To all our new employees: let's work hard together.

etymology: 「たち」 is written 「達」. In old Japanese it was an honorific plural suffix for gods and nobles, as in 「公達（きんだち）」. Its respectful nuance gradually faded, and it became a general plural suffix for people.
formation: 「たち」 is written 「達」 and was originally an honorific plural suffix for gods and nobles. The structure is simple: a noun referring to a person + a plural marker, so 「私＋たち」 = “the group centred on me”. Its core is “a group represented by someone”, not a mechanical “more than one”; that is why 「田中さんたち」 means Tanaka's group, and why it is usually left off when a number is already given. Because it began as a way of referring to people, it attaches in principle only to people; its respect faded over time, so with superiors you switch to the more polite 「方（がた）」.

similar.title: 〜ら (plural)
similar.explanation: 「ら」 also marks the plural (「彼ら」, 「僕ら」, 「これら」). It is more casual than 「たち」 and, used about others, can sound slightly dismissive. 「ら」 can also be used for things (「これら」), whereas 「たち」 is in principle only for people.

similar.title: 〜や〜など
similar.explanation: 「など」 means “and so on” and picks examples from a set; it works for both people and things. Name + 「たち」 means “X and company”, a group centred on that person. 「田中さんたちが来た」 focuses on that group; 「田中さんや鈴木さんなどが来た」 focuses on listing who came.

meaning: Attached to the masu-stem of a verb, it makes a noun meaning “how to ...” or “way of ...ing”.

senses.label: How to ...
senses.meaning: The method or steps for doing something: “how to ...”. The object particle 「を」 changes to 「の」.
senses.connection: Verb masu-stem + 方 (漢字を書く → 漢字の書き方)
examples: Please tell me how to read this kanji.
I don't know how to get to the station.
Making curry is easy.

senses.label: Way of ...ing
senses.meaning: A person's manner, style or habit of doing something, often used when describing others.
senses.connection: 話し方・考え方・歩き方・生き方, etc. + が／は
examples: That teacher has a gentle way of speaking.
Ways of thinking differ from person to person.

senses.label: With する verbs
senses.meaning: For する verbs like 「勉強する」, say 「noun + の + 仕方」 to mean “how to ...”.
senses.connection: Action noun + の + 仕方 (しかた)
examples: Please teach me how to study Japanese.
I don't really understand how to operate this machine.

notes: 「〜方」 turns the whole phrase into a noun, so the original 「を」 becomes 「の」: ✕「漢字を書き方」→ ○「漢字の書き方」.
You can't add 「方」 directly to a する verb: ✕「勉強し方」→ ○「勉強の仕方（しかた）」.
After an adjective or the た-form, 「方」 is read 「ほう」 and means something completely different: 「行った方（ほう）がいい」 = you'd better go, 「大きい方（ほう）」 = the bigger one. Neither means “the way of ...”.

daily.title: Asking for directions
daily.description: Asking station staff how to get somewhere.
daily.example: Excuse me, could you tell me how to get to Tokyo Station?

daily.title: Learning to cook
daily.description: Asking a friend how to make a dish.
daily.example: Can you teach me how to make this dish?

daily.title: Using a new phone
daily.description: You got a new phone and can't figure out a feature.
daily.example: I don't know how to use this app.

work.title: Training a newcomer
work.description: A senior colleague shows a new employee how to use the copier.
work.example: Let me explain how to use the copier.

work.title: Improving how you work
work.description: Your boss suggests changing the way work is done.
work.example: Let's review the way we go about our work.

etymology: 「方」 originally means “direction, side”. Attached to a verb stem, it went from “the direction of doing something” to “the way of doing something”. This use already existed in the Heian period.
formation: 「方」 originally means “direction, side”. A verb's ます-stem can already act as a noun meaning “this action” (「書き」 = the act of writing); adding 「方」 gives “the direction or path of writing” → the way or method of writing. Since 「書き方」 as a whole is a noun, the verb's object marker 「を」 has to become the noun modifier 「の」 (「漢字の書き方」), and it is followed by 「が」, 「を」 or 「は」. The stem of 「する」 is 「し」, and 「し＋方」 is 「仕方」, which is why a する verb becomes 「勉強の仕方」.

similar.title: 〜よう (manner)
similar.explanation: 「〜よう」 also attaches to the ます-stem to mean “way, manner”, as in 「話しよう」 or 「書きよう」, close to 「〜方」, but it is more literary and mostly found in set phrases (「物は言いよう」). For everyday “how to” questions, always use 「〜方」.

similar.title: 〜ようがない
similar.explanation: 「〜ようがない」 = “there is no way to ...” (「連絡しようがない」); the 「よう」 here means “method”. “I don't know how to do it” is 「やり方がわからない」; “there's simply nothing I can do about it” is 「やりようがない」.

meaning: The adverb 「あまり」 with a negative means “not very, not much”: the degree or frequency is low.
connection: あまり + negative form of verb / adjective

senses.label: Not very (degree)
senses.meaning: The degree is low: “not very ..., not that ...”. It sounds softer than a plain negative.
senses.connection: あまり + い-adjective 〜くない／な-adjective 〜じゃない
examples: This movie wasn't very interesting.
It's not very cold today, is it?
I don't really like spicy food.

senses.label: Not often (frequency)
senses.meaning: The frequency is low: “don't ... much, rarely ...”.
senses.connection: あまり + verb ない-form／ません
examples: I don't drink much.
I haven't been watching much TV lately.

senses.label: Can't really / don't really understand
senses.meaning: With negative potential verbs or 「わかる」, it means “can't ... very well” or “don't really understand”.
senses.connection: あまり + わからない／できない／negative potential verb
examples: I still can't speak Japanese very well.
I didn't really understand the explanation.

notes: Drop the negative and the meaning flips to “too ...”: 「あまり高くない」 = not very expensive, 「あまりに（も）高い」 = far too expensive.
When asked for their opinion, Japanese people often use 「あまり〜ない」 to say no gently. Saying 「全然おいしくない」 or 「まずい」 outright is very hurtful, especially to someone who cooked for you or gave you a present.
「あんまり」 is colloquial; with superiors, clients or in formal settings say 「あまり」.

daily.title: Commenting on food
daily.description: A friend asks if the food is good, and you gently say it's so-so.
daily.example: Hmm, it's not that good, I guess.

daily.title: Talking about hobbies
daily.description: A friend invites you to karaoke, and you say you're not a great singer.
daily.example: I'm not very good at singing.

daily.title: Talking about your routine
daily.description: Describing your eating habits when introducing yourself.
daily.example: I don't usually eat breakfast.

work.title: Giving a cautious opinion
work.description: Expressing reservations about a proposal in a meeting.
work.example: I don't think this plan is very realistic.

work.title: Saying you're short on time
work.description: Telling a coworker you don't have much time.
work.example: I don't have much time today, so please keep it brief.

etymology: 「あまり」 is written 「余り」, the stem of the verb 「余る」 (to be left over, to be excessive). It originally meant “the leftover part; too much”. With a negative, “not too much” became “not very ...”. 「あんまり」 is its emphatic spoken form.
formation: 「あまり」 is the noun form of the verb 「余る」 (to be left over, to exceed), originally “excess, too much”. 「あまり〜ない」 literally says “not to an excessive degree”, i.e. “some, but not much” → “not very”. Since it denies only the “excess” part and leaves room for “a little”, it sounds softer than 「全然〜ない」 and is often used to say no indirectly. Without a negative, 「あまりに（も）〜」 keeps the original sense of “excess” and means “too ...”.

similar.title: 〜ぜんぜん〜ない
similar.explanation: 「全然〜ない」 is “not at all”, a total denial; 「あまり〜ない」 is “not very”, leaving some room. 「あまり飲まない」 = I don't drink much; 「全然飲まない」 = I don't drink a drop.

similar.title: ちっとも〜ない
similar.explanation: 「ちっとも」 = “not in the least”, almost as strong as 「全然」, and in speech it often sounds annoyed (「ちっとも来ない」). 「あまり」 is calm and just says the degree isn't high.

similar.title: 〜あまり（に）
similar.explanation: Same origin: 「あまりに（も）〜」 followed by a positive means “too, excessively” (「あまりに高くて買えない」); this entry, 「あまり〜ない」 with a negative, means “not very”. Both come from 「余る」 — one says “too much”, the other “not as far as too much”.

meaning: The adverb 「ぜんぜん」 (全然) with a negative means “not at all, not in the least”.
connection: ぜんぜん (全然) + negative form of verb / adjective

senses.label: Not at all (degree)
senses.meaning: Completely denies a degree: “not at all, not in the least”. Much stronger than 「あまり〜ない」.
senses.connection: 全然 + い-adjective 〜くない／な-adjective 〜じゃない
examples: This test wasn't difficult at all.
This area isn't quiet at all, even at night.

senses.label: Not at all (actions)
senses.meaning: Doesn't do something at all, or can't do it at all. Often used with 「わからない」, 「できない」, etc.
senses.connection: 全然 + verb ない-form／ません／negative potential verb
examples: I don't understand French at all.
I couldn't sleep at all last night.
I haven't exercised at all recently.

senses.label: Casual: totally fine
senses.meaning: 「全然大丈夫」 and 「全然いい」 are common casual emphatic phrases meaning “totally fine”. Strict grammar says a negative should follow, so avoid this in formal situations.
senses.connection: 全然 + 大丈夫／平気／OK (casual)
examples: It's totally fine if you're late. Don't worry about it.

notes: Saying 「全然おいしくない」 or 「全然だめ」 about someone's cooking, work or present is very hurtful. Soften a negative opinion with 「あまり…」 or 「ちょっと…」.
「全然」 + positive (「全然大丈夫」) is only for casual talk among friends. With superiors and clients say 「まったく問題ございません」 or 「大丈夫です」.
In casual speech 「こっちの方が全然いい」 means “this one is way better” — it's emphasis, not negation, so don't read it as “not good at all”.

daily.title: After an exam
daily.description: A friend asks how your exam went.
daily.example: I totally blew it...

daily.title: Reassuring a friend
daily.description: A friend apologizes for being late, and you say you don't mind.
daily.example: I don't mind at all.

daily.title: Watching a foreign film
daily.description: Watching a foreign movie without subtitles, you can't follow it.
daily.example: Without subtitles, I don't understand it at all.

work.title: Reporting a delay
work.description: Admitting to your boss that you haven't really started.
work.example: I'm very sorry, I haven't made any progress at all yet.

work.title: Responding to a client's apology
work.description: A client apologizes for bothering you, and you reply politely.
work.example: No, it's no problem at all.

etymology: 「全然」 is a loanword from Chinese meaning “completely”. In the Meiji era it was used with both positive and negative verbs, but the pairing with a negative became the norm. Recently, 「全然 + positive」 has become common again in casual speech.
formation: 「全然」 is made of 「全」 (whole) + 「然」 (in the manner of), originally “completely, entirely”. Paired with a negative it means “completely not ...”, a total denial. 「全然」 itself only means “completely” and contains no negation, so in the Meiji era it could also go with positives; later its use with negatives became overwhelming, and people came to treat it as an adverb that requires a negative. In modern speech, 「全然大丈夫」 and 「全然いい」 use it again simply as “completely, by far” for emphasis — a return to its original meaning.

similar.title: まったく〜ない
similar.explanation: 「まったく〜ない」 means the same as 「全然〜ない」 but is more written and formal, used in writing and in business; 「全然」 is colloquial. With a client, 「まったく問題ありません」 is more appropriate than 「全然問題ないです」.

similar.title: ちっとも〜ない
similar.explanation: 「ちっとも」 also means “not at all”; it is colloquial and often sounds annoyed or complaining. Unlike 「全然」, it can't be used with a positive (✕「ちっとも大丈夫」).

similar.title: すこしも〜ない
similar.explanation: 「少しも〜ない」 literally means “not even a little” and has the same meaning as 「全然〜ない」, but it is more neutral and fine in both writing and speech; 「全然」 is the most common in conversation.

similar.title: 〜あまり〜ない
similar.explanation: 「あまり〜ない」 is “not very” and only says the degree is low; 「全然〜ない」 is “not at all”, a complete denial. Use 「あまり」 when you want to be gentle.

meaning: “Not ... yet”. An action that is planned or expected still hasn't happened.
connection: まだ + verb te-form + いない／いません

senses.label: Haven't done it yet
senses.meaning: An action isn't finished yet, but will or should be later. Use 「〜ていない」, not 「〜なかった」.
senses.connection: まだ + verb te-form + いない／いません (casual: 〜てない)
examples: I haven't finished my homework yet.
I haven't eaten dinner yet.
I haven't seen that movie yet.

senses.label: Answer: not yet
senses.meaning: A negative answer to 「もう〜ましたか」. You can simply say 「いいえ、まだです」.
senses.connection: いいえ、まだです／まだ〜ていません
examples: No, not yet.
“Have you had lunch yet?” “No, I haven't eaten yet.”

senses.label: Hasn't happened / arrived yet
senses.meaning: With 「来る」, 「届く」, 「決まる」, etc., something expected hasn't happened yet.
senses.connection: まだ + 来ていない／届いていない／決まっていない, etc.
examples: The package hasn't arrived yet.
Tanaka hasn't come yet.

notes: “Haven't done it yet” can't be said with the past negative: ✕「まだ食べなかった」→ ○「まだ食べていない」. If asked 「もう食べましたか」, answering 「いいえ、食べませんでした」 sounds like “I didn't eat (at that time) / I'm not going to”; say 「いいえ、まだです」.
Chasing a superior or client with 「まだですか」 or 「まだ送っていないんですか」 sounds impatient and accusing. Say 「〜の件、いかがでしょうか」 instead.
Take away the negative and the meaning changes completely: 「まだ雨が降っている」 = it's still raining, 「まだ雨が降っていない」 = it hasn't started raining yet.

daily.title: A friend asks if you've seen it
daily.description: A friend recommends a drama and asks if you've watched it.
daily.example: Sorry, I haven't seen it yet.

daily.title: A parent asks about homework
daily.description: A mother asks her child whether homework is done.
daily.example: You haven't finished your homework yet?

daily.title: Waiting for a friend
daily.description: Your friend still hasn't shown up, so you call.
daily.example: You haven't gotten to the station yet?

work.title: Checking on an email
work.description: Your boss asks whether you've replied to the client.
work.example: I'm sorry, I haven't replied yet.

work.title: Explaining something undecided
work.description: A client asks about the meeting date, and you say it's not set.
work.example: The schedule hasn't been decided yet.

etymology: 「まだ」 is generally thought to come from the old word 「いまだ」 (未だ), with the 「い」 dropped. It means “still, up to now”. Combined with 「〜ていない」, it means “still not done up to now”.
formation: 「まだ」 (「未だ」) means “still, up to now”, and 「〜ていない」 is the negative of 「〜ている」 (the result of a completed action continuing), meaning “not currently in the done state”. Together: “up to this moment, still not in the completed state” → “not ... yet”. Because it describes the present state, you must use 「〜ていない」, not 「〜なかった」, which points to a moment in the past. 「まだ」 also implies “it's expected to happen later”, so the pattern is typically used for things that are supposed to or are going to be done.

similar.title: 〜ている
similar.explanation: 「〜ていない」 is simply the negative of 「〜ている」: “not currently in the done state”. 「まだ〜ている」 (positive) means “still ...ing”; 「まだ〜ていない」 means “not ... yet”.

similar.title: なかなか〜ない
similar.explanation: 「なかなか〜ない」 means something you're waiting for “just won't happen”, with a sense of impatience (「バスがなかなか来ない」); 「まだ〜ていない」 just objectively says it hasn't been done so far.

similar.title: 〜たことがある
similar.explanation: Its negative 「〜たことがない」 means “have never ...” and is about life experience; 「まだ〜ていない」 is about something planned that hasn't been done yet. 「まだ見ていない」 implies you'll see it later; 「見たことがない」 just says you've never had that experience.

title: 〜もう〜た (already)
meaning: The adverb 「もう」 with the past form 「〜た／〜ました」 means “already”: an action is done or a state has changed.

senses.label: Already done
senses.meaning: An action is already finished: “have already ...”. It often implies “sooner than expected” or “no need to do it again”.
senses.connection: もう + verb ta-form／ました
examples: I've already finished my homework.
Tanaka has already gone home.
I've already read that book.

senses.label: Asking if it's done
senses.meaning: 「もう〜ましたか」 asks whether something is done yet. Answer yes with 「はい、もう〜ました」 and no with 「いいえ、まだです」.
senses.connection: もう + verb ました + か
examples: Have you had lunch yet?
Did you buy the tickets yet?

senses.label: Already (time or state)
senses.meaning: With a time or state noun, it means a time has already come or a state has changed, often with surprise: “already!” or “it's time to ...”.
senses.connection: もう + noun + だ／です (もう十二時だ)
examples: It's already twelve. Let's go to bed.
It's already spring, isn't it?

notes: 「もう」 with a negative means “no longer”, not “not yet”: 「もう食べない」 = I won't eat any more, 「まだ食べていない」 = I haven't eaten yet. Mixing them up changes the meaning completely.
For a negative answer, don't say ✕「いいえ、まだ食べませんでした」; say 「いいえ、まだです」 or 「まだ食べていません」.
Replying 「もう送りました」 when someone follows up can sound irritated; with clients, 「すでにお送りしております」 is more appropriate. Questions in the form 「もう〜の？」, like 「もう帰るの？」, also often carry surprise or reproach.
The 「もう」 in 「もう少し」, 「もう一度」 and 「もう一つ」 means “more, again”, and 「もうすぐ」 means “soon” — none of them mean “already”.

daily.title: Asking a friend about lunch
daily.description: Running into a friend at noon and asking if they've eaten.
daily.example: Have you eaten yet?

daily.title: Surprised by the time
daily.description: Chatting with a friend late into the night, you suddenly notice the time.
daily.example: What, it's already eleven!

daily.title: Updating your family
daily.description: Your family tells you to hurry and pack, and you say you're ready.
daily.example: I'm already ready.

work.title: Checking work is done
work.description: Your boss checks whether the documents have been sent.
work.example: Have you sent the documents yet?

work.title: Saying someone has left
work.description: A visitor asks for a coworker, and you say he's gone home.
work.example: Suzuki has already left for the day.

etymology: 「もう」 is generally thought to come from a change of the old adverb 「いま」 (今, now), meaning “by now, even more”. With the past tense it means “already”; with a number it means “more, another”.
formation: 「もう」 expresses that “things have already crossed a certain line and moved on”, and 「〜た」 marks completion. Together: “before the moment of speaking, things had already moved over to the completed side” → “already ...”. Because the core of 「もう」 is “crossing a line, one step further”, it can also go with numbers to mean “more” (「もう一つ」) and with negatives to mean “no longer” (「もう〜ない」) — only the line being crossed is different. And since it implies “past the expected point in time”, 「もう〜た」 often feels like “sooner than I thought”.

similar.title: 〜たばかり
similar.explanation: 「〜たばかり」 stresses “have just ...”, very close to the moment of completion (「来たばかり」); 「もう〜た」 only states that it's done, often with a nuance of “earlier than expected”.

similar.title: 〜ところだ
similar.explanation: 「〜たところだ」 means “have just finished (at this very moment)”, focusing on the stage of the action; 「もう〜た」 focuses on the fact that it's already done, whether just now or not.

similar.title: 〜てしまう
similar.explanation: 「〜てしまった」 means the action is completely finished, or carries regret; it often combines with 「もう」: 「もう全部食べてしまった」. 「もう〜た」 itself carries no regret.

title: 〜question word + か (indefinite)
meaning: A question word + 「か」 means an unspecified “some ...”: something, someone, somewhere, sometime.
connection: Question word (何・誰・どこ・いつ・どれ, etc.) + か

senses.label: Something, someone, somewhere
senses.meaning: A person, thing, place or time the speaker isn't sure of or doesn't need to specify: “something, someone, somewhere, sometime” (not a question). 「が」 and 「を」 are usually dropped; 「へ」, 「に」 and 「で」 can stay.
senses.connection: 何か・誰か・どこか (へ／に／で)・いつか
examples: I want something to drink.
Someone's here.
Did you go anywhere over the weekend?

senses.label: Some, a few
senses.meaning: 「いくつか」, 「何人か」, 「何回か」, etc. mean an unspecified small number: “some, a few, a few times, a few people”.
senses.connection: いくつか・いくらか・何人か・何回か・何日か, etc.
examples: I have a few questions.
I've been to Japan a few times.

senses.label: One of them
senses.meaning: 「どれか」 and 「どちらか」 mean an unspecified one of several: “any one, one of them”.
senses.connection: どれか・どちらか (+ を／が)
examples: Please choose one from these.
Please pick one of the two.

notes: 「どこかへ行きましたか」 asks “Did you go anywhere?”, so answer 「はい／いいえ」 first; 「どこへ行きましたか」 asks “Where did you go?”. Mixing them up means answering the wrong question.
Negative sentences normally use 「何も〜ない」, not 「何か」: ✕「何か食べませんでした」→ ○「何も食べませんでした」. 「何か食べませんか」, on the other hand, is an invitation: “Shall we eat something?”
Don't use 「誰か」 for superiors or clients; say 「どなたか」: 「どなたかいらっしゃいますか」. Colloquial 「なんか」 also sounds casual; in business say 「何かご質問はございますか」.

daily.title: Asking family at home
daily.description: You're hungry and ask if there's anything to eat.
daily.example: Is there anything to eat?

daily.title: Calling for help
daily.description: You're in trouble on the street and shout for help.
daily.example: Somebody help me!

daily.title: Promising something for the future
daily.description: Promising a friend to travel together someday.
daily.example: Let's go to Kyoto together someday.

work.title: Before a meeting ends
work.description: The chair checks if anyone has questions.
work.example: Are there any questions?

work.title: Finding a helper
work.description: Your boss asks the team to send someone to help.
work.example: Is there anyone who can help?

etymology: 「か」 was originally a particle of question and uncertainty. After a question word, it turns “what is it?” into “some uncertain thing”. This use already existed in old Japanese.
formation: A question word stands for “the unknown one”, and 「か」 expresses uncertainty. Question word + 「か」 = “some one, I don't know which”, turning the question word from asking into pointing at an unspecified thing. So 「何か」 and 「誰か」 work as a single noun and can be the subject or object (「が」 and 「を」 are often dropped), and the sentence itself doesn't have to be a question. With the same question words, 「も」 gives “every one / none”, and 「でも」 gives “any one will do” — the meaning is decided by the particle that follows.

similar.title: 〜でも (question word + でも)
similar.explanation: The same question words + 「でも」 mean “anything / anyone at all” (「何でもいい」); + 「か」 just means “some one” (「何かほしい」). The former is all-inclusive, the latter indefinite.

similar.title: 〜question word + も〜ない (total negation)
similar.explanation: The same question words + 「も」 together with a negative mean “nothing, nobody” (「何もない」). If asked 「何かありますか」, the negative answer is 「何もありません」.

similar.title: 〜か何か
similar.explanation: 「〜か何か」 is 「か」 + 「何か」 and means “... or something”, as in 「コーヒーか何か飲みませんか」. It gives one example while leaving room for others, whereas 「何か」 on its own specifies nothing at all.

title: 〜question word + も〜ない (total negation)
meaning: A question word + 「も」 with a negative gives total negation: “nothing, nobody, nowhere”.
connection: Question word (+ particle) + も + negative form of verb / adjective

senses.label: Nothing, nobody
senses.meaning: 「何も」 and 「誰も」 replace 「が」 and 「を」 for total negation: “not anything, not anyone”.
senses.connection: 何も／誰も + negative form
examples: I didn't eat anything this morning.
There's nobody in the classroom.
I don't understand anything.

senses.label: Particle + も
senses.meaning: When you need 「に」, 「へ」, 「で」, 「と」, etc., put the particle between the question word and 「も」: 「どこにも」, 「誰とも」, 「どこへも」.
senses.connection: どこにも・どこへも・誰にも・誰とも・何にも + negative form
examples: I didn't go anywhere on Sunday.
Don't tell anyone about this, okay?
I can't find my keys anywhere.

senses.label: Neither, none of them
senses.meaning: 「どれも」 and 「どちらも」 with a negative mean none of the options: “none of them, neither”.
senses.connection: どれも／どちらも + negative form
examples: I don't like any of them.
Both are too expensive, so I can't buy either.

notes: Other particles go between the question word and 「も」: ✕「どこもに行かない」→ ○「どこにも行かない」; ✕「誰もと話さない」→ ○「誰とも話さない」. 「が」 and 「を」 simply drop out: ✕「誰がも」.
「何も」 and 「何でも」 are opposites: 「何も食べません」 = I eat nothing, 「何でも食べます」 = I eat anything.
When a host serves food saying 「何もありませんが、どうぞ」, it is a humble set phrase (“it's nothing special, but please help yourself”), not a literal statement — don't take it at face value or agree with it.

daily.title: Empty fridge
daily.description: You open the fridge and find nothing.
daily.example: There's nothing in the fridge.

daily.title: Talking about the weekend
daily.description: A friend asks where you went over the weekend.
daily.example: I didn't go anywhere this weekend.

daily.title: Keeping a secret
daily.description: You tell a friend a secret and ask them not to tell anyone.
daily.example: Don't tell anyone, okay?

work.title: Checking in a meeting
work.description: The chair asks for comments, and nobody has any.
work.example: There are no particular problems.

work.title: No one answering
work.description: You call a client, but nobody is in their office.
work.example: I called several times, but nobody answered.

etymology: 「も」 originally means “also”. After a question word it means “whatever it is, also ...”, and with a negative it becomes total negation, “nothing at all”. This use already existed in old Japanese.
formation: A question word refers to “any possible one”, and 「も」 means “also, all included”, so together they mean “whichever one it is, ... too”. Combined with a negative, this becomes “whichever one it is, not ...” — a total negation. Since 「も」 itself only means “all included” and contains no negation, 「どれも」 and 「誰も」 with a positive mean “all ...” (「どれもおいしい」). Particles like 「に」, 「と」 and 「へ」 are kept and placed between the question word and 「も」 (「誰にも」), because 「も」 is added to the whole unit “question word + particle”.

similar.title: 〜question word + か (indefinite)
similar.explanation: The same question words + 「か」 mean “something, someone” (「誰か来た」) and are not negative; + 「も」 together with a negative they give a total negation (「誰も来ない」).

similar.title: 〜でも (question word + でも)
similar.explanation: 「何でも」 and 「誰でも」 are all-inclusive positives, “anything / anyone at all”; 「何も〜ない」 is a total negative. Mind the reading: 「何でも」 is 「なんでも」, 「何も」 is 「なにも」.

similar.title: 〜ぜんぜん〜ない
similar.explanation: 「全然〜ない」 negates the degree (“not at all”); 「何も〜ない」 negates the object (“not a single thing”). 「全然食べない」 stresses “I don't eat at all”; 「何も食べない」 stresses “I don't eat a single thing”.

meaning: “Please give me ...”. Used to ask for things when shopping, ordering food, etc.
connection: Noun + を (+ quantity) + ください

senses.label: Please give me (a thing)
senses.meaning: Politely asks someone for a thing. Common in shops, restaurants and at counters: “... please”.
senses.connection: Noun + を + ください
examples: Water, please.
Excuse me, could I have the menu?
I'll take this one.

senses.label: Saying how many
senses.meaning: Put the quantity between 「を」 and 「ください」 to say how many you want.
senses.connection: Noun + を + quantity + ください
examples: Three apples, please.
Five stamps, please.

senses.label: Casual: dropping を, friendly form
senses.meaning: In speech, 「を」 is often dropped. With family and friends, you can use the more casual 「ちょうだい」.
senses.connection: Noun / quantity + ください; noun + (を) ちょうだい
examples: Two coffees, please.
Mom, can I have that snack?

notes: Saying 「資料をください」 to a superior or client sounds like an order; say 「資料をいただけますか」 or 「資料をお願いできますか」.

「〜をください」 asks only for things; to ask someone to do something, use the te-form — get it wrong and the meaning changes completely: 「お茶をください」 = please give me some tea, 「お茶を入れてください」 = please make me some tea.
Put the number after 「を」: 「りんごを三つください」; ✕「三つのりんごをください」 sounds very unnatural.
「ちょうだい」 is only for family and very close friends; using it with anyone else sounds childish and rude.

daily.title: At a convenience store
daily.description: Asking for a bag at the register.
daily.example: A bag, please.

daily.title: Ordering at a restaurant
daily.description: Ordering from the menu.
daily.example: I'll have this lunch set.

daily.title: Buying tickets at a station
daily.description: Saying how many tickets you need at the counter.
daily.example: Two tickets to Osaka, please.

work.title: Asking a coworker for a handout
work.description: During a meeting, asking a coworker to pass you a copy.
work.example: Could I have a copy of that document?

work.title: Asking for a reply
work.description: Asking someone to reply by email or phone (fairly casual; in formal settings use 「お返事をいただけますか」).
work.example: Please send me a reply.

etymology: 「ください」 comes from 「くだされ」, the imperative of the verb 「くださる」 (下さる, “to bestow”). 「くださる」 originally meant “(a superior) gives to (an inferior)”, so 「〜をください」 literally means “please bestow ... on me”.
formation: 「を」 marks the thing you want, and 「ください」 is the imperative of 「くださる」 (“a superior gives to me”). The whole sentence means “please bestow (this thing) on me”, so the direction of giving is fixed as “you → me”, and it can only be used to ask the other person for something. Because 「くださる」 is itself respectful language, 「ください」 has a basic level of politeness; but it is still an imperative and sounds direct to superiors and clients, so for more politeness you switch to the question form 「いただけますか」.

similar.title: 〜をお願いします
similar.explanation: 「〜をお願いします」 is softer and more polite than 「〜をください」 and can also be used for services and actions (「タクシーをお願いします」); 「ください」 is mainly for things and sounds more direct. Both are fine when ordering in a shop.

similar.title: 〜てください
similar.explanation: Same origin: 「ください」 after a verb's te-form asks the other person to do an action (「見てください」); after a noun + 「を」 it asks them to give you a thing (「水をください」).

similar.title: 〜がほしい
similar.explanation: 「〜がほしい」 only states your own wish and doesn't actually ask anyone (「新しい靴がほしい」); 「〜をください」 is a direct request to the person in front of you. Saying 「水がほしい」 to a waiter is unnatural; say 「水をください」.

meaning: “... please / could you ...”. A polite way to ask for things or services, with a wider range than 「〜をください」.
connection: Noun + を + お願いします (more polite: お願いいたします)

senses.label: Ordering and shopping
senses.meaning: Politely asking for things or ordering in restaurants and shops. Softer and more polite than 「〜をください」.
senses.connection: Noun (+ quantity) + を + お願いします
examples: One hot coffee, please.
Check, please.
This one, please.

senses.label: Asking for a service
senses.meaning: Asks someone to provide a service or do something. The object can be abstract: “could you ...?”.
senses.connection: タクシー・チェックイン・説明・確認, etc. + を + お願いします
examples: Could you call a taxi for me, please?
I'd like to check in, please.
Please confirm by tomorrow.

senses.label: Asking for someone on the phone
senses.meaning: On the phone, asks to speak to someone: “May I speak to ...?”.
senses.connection: Person's name (+ さん) + を + お願いします／お願いできますか
examples: May I speak to Mr. Tanaka in the sales department, please?

notes: When asking a client to do something, put 「ご／お」 in front of the action noun: 「確認をお願いします」→「ご確認をお願いいたします」, 「ご連絡をお願いいたします」.

When phoning another company and asking for someone, say 「営業部の田中様をお願いいたします」. Conversely, when you mention a colleague from your own company to an outsider — even your boss — drop honorifics like 「さん」 or 「部長」: ✕「田中部長は外出中です」→ ○「田中は外出しております」.
「〜をお願いします」 makes the request with a noun, so no verb can come before it: ✕「確認するをお願いします」→ ○「確認をお願いします」 or 「確認してください」.

work.title: Calling for someone
work.description: Calling a client's company and asking to be put through to the person in charge.
work.example: Sorry to bother you, but may I speak to Mr. Yamada, the department manager?

work.title: Asking for confirmation by email
work.description: Asking a client to check an attachment in a business email.
work.example: Please review the attached documents.

work.title: Asking for help
work.description: Asking a coworker to help with a task.
work.example: Could you help me with this matter?

etymology: 「お願い」 is the noun form of the verb 「願う」 (to wish, to request) with the polite prefix 「お」. 「します」 is the polite form of 「する」. Literally, it means “I make a request to you”.
formation: 「お願い」 is the beautifying prefix 「お」 + the stem of the verb 「願う」 (to wish, to request), forming the noun “a request”; 「します」 is the polite form of 「する」. The structure is “I put forward (this noun) as a request”, i.e. “I ask you to give me / do for me ...”. Since the object is just “the content of the request”, it can be a thing (「コーヒー」) or a service or action (「確認」, 「説明」), so it covers more ground than 「ください」. 「お＋stem＋する」 is itself a humble pattern in which the speaker lowers themselves, so it sounds softer than the imperative 「ください」; replace 「する」 with the humble 「いたす」 and you get the even more formal 「お願いいたします」.

similar.title: 〜をください
similar.explanation: 「〜をください」 asks for a thing directly and sounds fairly blunt; 「〜をお願いします」 is more polite and can also be used for services and actions (「説明をお願いします」). Either is fine with shop staff; with clients and superiors use 「お願いします」.

similar.title: 〜ていただけませんか
similar.explanation: 「〜ていただけませんか」 asks someone to do something in question form and is even softer and more courteous than 「〜をお願いします」, suitable for asking a favour beyond the usual. 「確認をお願いします」 ≈ 「確認していただけませんか」, the latter being more deferential.

similar.title: お〜ください
similar.explanation: 「ご確認ください」 and 「お待ちください」 also politely ask someone to do something, but they are still imperatives and are mostly used on signs, in announcements and in customer service. In emails, asking someone to do something is usually 「ご確認をお願いいたします」, which sounds softer.
